item.title: Globalizing Intelligence: Orchestrating Artificial Intelligence for Global Advantage
item.content:encoded:
Julian Birkinshaw, Ivey Business School

Valérie Duplat, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Saeed Khanagha, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Oli Mihalache, Athabasca University

Shaker Zahra, University of Minnesota

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping how multinational enterprises and international new ventures compete globally. This special issue seeks research exploring how AI technologies—particularly generative AI—enable new competitive strategies, from building proprietary AI capabilities to deploying AI tools for market analysis and decision-making. The call welcomes papers examining AI's impact on firm competitiveness, internationalization strategies, organizational transformation, and resilience in volatile environments.

The issue addresses three core dimensions through which AI influences global strategy. First, it considers how firms develop AI-centric capabilities that serve as sources of competitive advantage across borders. Second, it explores how organizations strategically deploy AI to interpret global markets and make faster, more informed decisions. Third, it examines how firms must redesign governance structures and navigate complex international regulatory frameworks to effectively harness AI across multiple countries and institutional contexts.

Appel publié par Global Strategy Journal. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do proprietary generative-AI capabilities influence entry mode choice in different host-country contexts?
  • What factors affect location for AI-centric MNEs and INV founders seeking global scale?
  • How do AI-centric firms calibrate the balance between global standardization of models and local adaptation to institutional and cultural distance?
  • How do AI-centric INVs build and scale proprietary capabilities to compete globally, and how do these digital-born assets challenge traditional views on firm-specific advantages and gradual internationalization?
  • How do AI-centric MNEs and INVs manage international scaling of generative-AI capabilities, and what role do global knowledge-transfer mechanisms play in enabling rapid diffusion across subsidiaries?
  • How do AI-centric MNEs manage cross-border complementarities between firm-specific data and host-country capabilities to build sustainable competitive advantage?
  • To what extent do open-core versus fully proprietary model strategies shape the boundary decisions (make, buy, ally) of AI-centric firms in different regulatory environments?
  • How do AI-centric firms mitigate liability of foreignness in AI ethics and bias by embedding local data and diverse cultural inputs into their global model-training pipelines?
  • How can AI-enabled research methods be leveraged by firms to better understand foreign market reception and inform internationalization strategies?
  • How do MNEs use generative-AI tools to refine entry-mode strategies (i.e., exporting, licensing, or FDI) by dynamically assessing host-market demand and regulatory complexity?
  • Under what conditions can AI-driven scenario planning replace or complement traditional market-selection frameworks (e.g., CAGE) for entering new countries?
  • How do firms leverage generative-AI-enabled localization (e.g., product design, marketing copy) to navigate cultural distance and strengthen local responsiveness in global integration strategies?
  • What capabilities must regional subsidiaries develop to interpret and act on AI-generated market insights, and how does this reshape subsidiary autonomy versus headquarters control?
  • How does generative AI affect the integration-responsiveness trade-off in global operations under geopolitical or natural-disaster shocks?
  • In what ways do AI-mediated customer-interaction platforms alter traditional service subsidiary roles and the governance of cross-border service delivery?
  • How do firms combine human judgment and AI recommendations in cross-border new product development alliances to balance exploration and exploitation?
  • How do AI-enabled INVs sense and respond to global market signals differently than incumbents, and how do AI tools help them to overcome limited experience in culturally or institutionally distant markets?
  • In what ways do AI-driven analytics of cultural signals and media content reshape how MNEs and INVs interpret foreign consumer preferences and adapt entry strategies?
  • How can methodological advances in AI-based content analysis contribute to more fine-grained monitoring of cultural distance and liability of foreignness in real time?
  • How do MNEs structure global AI governance bodies to balance headquarters-led oversight with subsidiary-level discretion across divergent institutional environments?
  • What alliance governance mechanisms (joint ventures, co-development agreements) best facilitate GDPR-compliant data-sharing for generative-AI co-creation between European and Asian partners?
  • How do emerging global AI regulations reshape MNEs' decisions on center-of-gravity for model deployment (cloud vs. on-prem) across host countries?
  • How do entrepreneurial ecosystems in emerging markets influence the design of cross-border data trusts and co-governance structures for INV-led AI initiatives?
  • How do platform partnerships with regional software ecosystems (e.g., Midjourney in European design suites, Eleven Labs in Asian media platforms) alter inter-firm governance and value-capture?
  • In what ways do pre-competitive data trusts and industry consortia mitigate institutional voids and enable co-governance of domain-specific generative models in emerging markets?
  • How must performance metrics and incentive systems evolve to reward cross-border AI collaboration while managing moral-hazard and knowledge-leakage risks?
  • What role do board-level AI oversight committees play in enforcing a cohesive global AI ethics framework amid diverse local legal and cultural norms?
  • How can AI-based methods be leveraged to examine how firms navigate cross-border governance and regulatory environments?

Timeline

  • September 15, 2026: Submission window opens
  • October 15, 2026: Deadline for submissions

  • Qian (Cecilia) Gu, Georgia State University

item.title: Trustworthy Content Governance and Safe Generative AI in the Age of Large Language Models
item.content:encoded:
This special issue addresses the challenges of governing content and ensuring safety in generative AI systems, particularly as large language models become increasingly prevalent. The issue seeks research on establishing trustworthy frameworks and mechanisms for managing content while developing safer generative AI technologies.

item.title: Measuring GenAI and Productivity in Work and Careers
item.content:encoded:
Generative AI is being increasingly integrated into workplace processes and career development, reshaping how tasks are executed and decisions are made. This presents significant questions about productivity measurement, particularly as work increasingly involves collaboration between humans and AI systems rather than purely human effort.

When humans and AI systems work together to produce outputs, it becomes challenging to determine what portion of results comes from human contribution versus AI assistance. This fundamental issue means that traditional concepts of productivity may no longer adequately capture work performance in AI-augmented contexts. The special issue seeks research that reconceptualizes how productivity should be defined and measured when human-AI collaboration is involved, with attention to career implications and organizational factors that influence these dynamics.

Appel publié par Personnel Review. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Conceptualizing productivity in AI work and careers
  • Distinguishing between AI exposure, use, and augmentation
  • Measuring human versus AI contributions to outputs and performance
  • Changes in the distribution of performance (e.g., effects on high and lower performers)
  • Implications of GenAI for skill development, career trajectories, and employability
  • The role of HR practices, job design, and organizational context in shaping productivity related to AI
  • Methodological approaches to studying AI and work (e.g., multi-source data, longitudinal designs, behavioral, other types of data)

item.title: Generative AI and Data Envelopment Analysis for Performance Measurement and Public Value
item.content:encoded:
This special issue explores the intersection of generative artificial intelligence and data envelopment analysis as tools for measuring organizational performance and creating public value. The collection seeks research that demonstrates how these technologies can enhance performance evaluation methodologies and provide insights into efficiency across various sectors, particularly in public organizations where value creation extends beyond traditional financial metrics.

  • Performance evaluation in public sector organizations

item.title: AI-driven marketing and Sustainability
item.content:encoded:
Pham Van Hau, Unitec Institute of Technology

Carolyn Strong, Cardiff University

Park Thaichon, University of Southern Queensland

This special issue focuses on the emerging intersection of artificial intelligence and sustainable marketing. AI technologies like machine learning and predictive analytics are rapidly transforming marketing practices, while sustainability challenges demand new approaches to shift consumption patterns and market systems. The special issue seeks research examining how AI-driven marketing influences sustainability outcomes at individual, organizational, and system-wide levels.

The integration of AI in marketing presents both opportunities and challenges for sustainability. AI tools can enable personalized sustainability nudges, improve resource efficiency, and support circular economy initiatives. However, concerns include algorithmic bias, privacy issues, transparency challenges, and the risk of reinforcing unsustainable consumption through hyper-personalized marketing. Understanding these dynamics is critical to ensure AI contributes positively to sustainable futures rather than exacerbating environmental and social challenges.

Appel publié par Journal of Strategic Marketing. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Relational pedagogies in an age of GenAI
item.content:encoded:
Karen Gravett, University of Surrey

Naomi Winstone, University of Surrey

Kieran Balloo, Southern Cross University

This special issue explores relational pedagogies—teaching practices emphasizing meaningful connections between teachers and students, and engagement with both human and nonhuman entities like digital technologies—within contemporary higher education contexts shaped by generative artificial intelligence. Relational pedagogies foster emotional and affective dimensions of education while challenging competitive individualistic approaches.

The rapid emergence of GenAI is fundamentally reshaping how educators and students interact, redefining educational practices politically, practically, and ideologically. The special issue seeks critical perspectives on how GenAI reconfigures relationality in higher education, addressing questions about student engagement with AI outside educator control, evolving assessment and feedback practices, care in digitalized contexts, equity implications, and the ethical and environmental concerns these technologies raise.

Appel publié par Teaching in Higher Education. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Discourses surrounding GenAI and pedagogy
  • Relationality with respect to assessment practices
  • Relational feedback processes

  • The intersection of AI technologies with notions of mattering and belonging
  • Research into academic work and relational connections
  • The materiality of education
  • Political and ethical questions regarding digital technologies such as surveillance, datafication, and agency
  • GenAI's environmental impacts and their intersection with pedagogical, ethical, and political questions
  • Posthuman, sociomaterial and feminist materialist perspectives
  • How does students' use of GenAI reshape relationships and pedagogies?
  • What role do emotions, affective relations, and embodied experiences play for students and educators in an age of GenAI?

item.title: Generative AI and New Methods of Inquiry in Information Systems Research
item.content:encoded:
Ahmed Abbasi, University of Notre Dame

Martin Bichler, Technical University of Munich

Ram Gopal, University of Warwick

Elena Karahanna, University of Georgia

Suprateek Sarker, University of Virginia

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping not only organizations, markets, and technologies, but also the practice of scientific research itself. Large language models, multimodal foundation models, and increasingly agentic AI systems now participate in activities such as literature discovery, theorizing, data analysis, simulation, coding, and writing.

This Special Issue seeks papers that push the boundaries of what can be achieved through innovative, rigorous, and responsible use of Generative AI in the information systems research process. Rather than focusing on GenAI solely as an object of empirical study, the SI emphasizes GenAI as a research collaborator, instrument, and infrastructure.

The ambition of the SI is twofold: to publish a small number of exemplary papers that demonstrate novel research capabilities enabled by GenAI, and to advance shared principles, frameworks, and practices that will shape how information systems research is conducted and reported in an era of human–AI collaboration.

Appel publié par Information Systems Research. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Hybrid human–AI workflows for coding, classification, or sensemaking
  • GenAI-supported measurement development, construct validation, or scale refinement
  • GenAI-supported survey design, sampling, and survey administration
  • GenAI-supported experimental design, treatment generation, and implementation
  • GenAI-supported computational theory construction
  • Simulation, agent-based modeling, or scenario generation
  • GenAI-enabled qualitative analysis, theory building, or inductive discovery
  • GenAI-assisted econometric modeling, estimation, or robustness analysis
  • AI-supported proof search, counterexample generation, or equilibrium exploration
  • Discovery or validation of analytical models using generative simulation
  • GenAI-assisted testing of operational utility and/or design validity
  • Design and evaluation of GenAI-based tools for IS research
  • Reproducible pipelines, benchmarks, and evaluation harnesses
  • Systems supporting transparency, provenance, and verification

item.title: AI Companions
item.content:encoded:
Raffaele Ciriello, The University of Sydney Business School

Martin Adam, University of Goettingen

Zhongyun Zhou, Tongji University

AI companions are conversational systems designed to simulate human-like relationships and deployed as emotional support tools, tutors, and therapeutic assistants. Unlike conventional productivity software, their value derives from sustained interaction and personalised continuity, raising questions about trust, dependency, wellbeing, and how relational dynamics emerge through interactions between users, systems, and contexts.

This special issue invites Information Systems scholarship to examine AI companions through a relational lens extending beyond efficiency metrics. While these systems offer potential benefits such as broadened access to support, they simultaneously raise concerns about surveillance, manipulation, and commodified intimacy, reshaping individual capabilities and organisational practices.

The special issue welcomes theoretically ambitious and empirically grounded research across diverse methodologies that carefully theorise the sociotechnical characteristics of relational AI systems. Submissions should address design, governance, and use implications, with particular interest in interdisciplinary and critical perspectives.

Appel publié par Information Systems Journal. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Communicating and Framing Innovation in the Era of Generative AI
item.content:encoded:
Saeedeh Ahmadi, University of Amsterdam

Saeed Khanagha, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Georg Reischauer, Leuphana University Lüneburg

Georg Reischauer, Johannes Kepler University Linz

Victor P Seidel, Babson College

Llewellyn D W Thomas, University of Sydney Business School

Llewellyn D W Thomas, Imperial College Business School

Innovation communication and framing are central to product development success across all stages, shaping how organizations coordinate internally and externally. Generative AI fundamentally disrupts traditional approaches to communicating and framing innovation, creating both opportunities and challenges. Firms are already experimenting creatively with these technologies, yet face significant risks including authenticity concerns, misinformation, and backlash from audiences skeptical of AI-generated content.

This special issue seeks interdisciplinary research examining how Generative AI shapes communication and framing of innovation at individual, organizational, industry, and ecosystem levels. Key areas include how AI-mediated communication transforms new product development processes, manages technological hype cycles, and navigates tensions between creativity and authenticity. The issue welcomes quantitative, qualitative, mixed-methods, and conceptual work across all innovation types and organizational contexts, with particular interest in research on non-venture firms including corporations, family businesses, and small-to-medium enterprises.

item.title: Generative AI and the Environment: How Can IS Scholars Contribute to Addressing the Problem and Identifying Solutions
item.content:encoded:
Marco Marabelli, Bentley University

Robert Davison, City University of Hong Kong

Federico Iannacci, University of Sussex

Shahla Ghobadi, University of Leeds

Zhongyun Zhou, Tongji University

Vanessa Cooper, RMIT University

This special issue examines how information systems scholarship can address environmental concerns related to generative AI. While GAI offers significant benefits for efficiency and automation, its rapid development has created substantial environmental challenges, including high electricity consumption, water use for cooling, and electronic waste from obsolete computing hardware. These impacts disproportionately affect vulnerable populations and regions in the Global South.

The issue seeks studies adopting an eco-socio-technical perspective to explore both the negative environmental effects of GAI and its potential benefits for weather forecasting, agriculture, and urban management. Contributors are encouraged to investigate how organizations, governments, individuals, and communities can implement and use GAI responsibly, examining tradeoffs between technological benefits and environmental costs. Research employing primary data, various methodologies, and practitioner perspectives are welcomed.

Appel publié par Information Systems Journal. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Local and global policies associated with data centers, outsourcing, and offshoring practices, including legal, managerial, and economic perspectives
  • Business models relying on or incentivizing GAI across specific industries such as healthcare, automotive, robotics, and aerospace, focusing on efficiency versus responsible use tradeoffs
  • Individual-level practices of responsible GAI use in organizational and private citizen contexts, and how users understand environmental consequences
  • GAI applications in smart cities, including traffic and parking optimization while addressing surveillance concerns
  • GAI use in public administrations to streamline processes such as document production and benefit eligibility checks
  • Existential short-term and long-term eco-socio-technical effects and the role of IS discipline in mitigating environmental and societal risks from large-scale GAI diffusion
  • Collective action and activism strategies for promoting green development and responsible GAI use by major technology developers and deployers

Timeline

  • December 31, 2026: Submission deadline for extended abstracts
  • June 30, 2027: Submission deadline for full papers

item.title: Socially Responsible Marketing with AI for Enhanced Consumer Experience Design
item.content:encoded:
Muhammad S. Akram, University of Essex

Boris Bartikowski, Kedge Business School

Neeru Malhotra, Georgia Southern University

Muhammad Awais Shakir Goraya, University of Portsmouth

This special issue examines how artificial intelligence, particularly generative AI and immersive technologies, is reshaping consumer experiences and marketing strategies. The collection addresses emerging challenges around consumer autonomy, data governance, and well-being as AI becomes increasingly embedded in phygital ecosystems that blend physical and digital touchpoints. The issue aims to establish a multidisciplinary foundation for integrating AI into socially responsible marketing practices that prioritize consumer trust, equity, and psychological safety.

The special issue seeks research that advances ethical frameworks for AI-driven marketing innovation, identifies how responsible practices create competitive advantage, develops multi-stakeholder collaboration approaches, and examines implications for vulnerable populations. It welcomes studies on algorithmic transparency, anthropomorphic AI relationships, identity formation in AI-mediated environments, and governance mechanisms that balance personalization with consumer protection across immersive and phygital contexts.

Appel publié par Psychology and Marketing. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How does generative AI influence consumer autonomy, trust and perceived control in immersive and phygital environments?
  • What design principles and governance mechanisms ensure that personalisation enhances rather than manipulates decision-making?
  • What mechanisms enable responsible AI to protect consumer agency while delivering personalisation benefits?
  • How do AI-powered AR filters and virtual avatars influence body image, self-esteem, and identity formation?
  • What ethical design principles ensure inclusive representation of race, gender, and ability in AI-generated avatars?
  • How can brands use immersive technologies responsibly to promote authentic identity expression rather than narrow beauty standards?
  • How can Socially Responsible Marketing (SRM) help prevent body image harm in AI-driven and immersive marketing environments?
  • How do consumer perceptions of algorithmic transparency and fairness influence trust in AI-driven experiences?
  • What communication strategies credibly signal ethical AI commitments to consumers?
  • How can responsible AI principles prevent deception and manipulation in the deployment of virtual influencers within socially responsible marketing?
  • How do anthropomorphism and mind-related attributions to AI shape consumer–AI relationships and their implications for well-being?
  • How does AI-driven orchestration of phygitality (integrated physical and digital experiences) influence consumer perceptions of responsibility, authenticity, and trust?
  • How do phygital service environments alter power asymmetries between firms and consumers?

  • August 31, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: The Generative Workplace: The Lived Experience of Generative AI at Work
item.content:encoded:
Louis Tay, Purdue University

Sarah Bankins, Macquarie University

Markus Langer, University of Freiburg

This special issue examines how generative AI is reshaping the subjective experience of work across individuals, teams, and organizations. Rather than focusing on technical capabilities, it centers on what it feels like to work with AI systems like ChatGPT and Claude—how these tools influence engagement, relationships, identity, and organizational norms as adoption rapidly increases among knowledge workers worldwide.

The issue seeks empirically rigorous, theory-grounded research that closely observes generative AI in actual workplace settings. Priority is given to field research within organizations, implementation studies tracking deployment experiences, longitudinal designs, and rigorous qualitative research. Vignette studies, cross-sectional surveys of convenience samples, and conceptual papers without data are out of scope.

Submissions should articulate theoretical mechanisms for how generative AI changes work experiences, provide evidence credible for practitioners, and explicitly discuss practical impact for employees, managers, HR leaders, and policymakers.

Appel publié par Personnel Psychology. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Experience of work: Cognitive offloading and changes in effort, flow, and engagement; experiences of autonomy, competence, and ownership over AI-generated or AI-assisted output; changes to the meaning of work; skill development versus skill atrophy; work intensification versus work-life balance; changing nature of expertise; calibration of trust and over- or under-reliance; professional identity as roles shift
  • Workplace relationships: Generative AI as a team member and its impact on social and working dynamics; emerging disclosure norms; trust, attribution, and competence judgments when AI is involved; migration of help-seeking and sensemaking from colleagues to AI tools; effects on collaboration, collegiality, reciprocity, informal mentorship, and organizational cohesion
  • Training and development: Use and experience of AI as a trainer, coach, and mentor; development and declines in knowledge, skills, and abilities with AI use; lasting effects of AI-based training; comparisons of human trainers versus AI trainers; design of AI-based training and transfer to job performance
  • Leadership: Leaders' use of generative AI for communication and the authenticity dilemma of machine-mediated empathy, vision, and feedback; leader decision processes with AI input; generative AI systems operating autonomously or in hybrid arrangements; what it feels like to be managed by generative AI
  • Organizational culture: Emergent norms of acceptable generative AI use; psychological safety around disclosing versus concealing use; experience of monitoring and surveillance of workers' AI use or non-use; equity and felt divide between users and non-users; implications for inclusive workplaces

Timeline

  • August 1, 2027: Submission window opens

item.title: Digital Transformation and Service
item.content:encoded:
Christian Bartelheimer, University of Göttingen

Daniel Beverungen, Paderborn University

Sara Hofmann, University of Agder

Lysanne Lessard, University of Ottawa

This topical collection examines how digital transformation and service shape contemporary information systems, particularly focusing on value creation across organizational boundaries through digital technologies, platforms, and ecosystems. The collection seeks theoretically grounded research that goes beyond broad claims about digital transformation to instead examine how IT artifacts are designed and applied to enable value co-creation in service contexts.

The collection prioritizes submissions that explicitly analyze IT artifacts rather than treating them as black boxes, showing how these artifacts shape and are shaped by organizational digital transformation. Research should be grounded in IS literature and address relevant gaps for both theory and practice, with particular interest in inter-organizational and platform-based service scenarios relevant to Electronic Markets.

Appel publié par Electronic Markets. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Digital transformation and service in information systems
  • Design and application of IT artifacts for value co-creation
  • Smart service systems and ecosystems at multiple levels (communities, organizations, inter-organizational arrangements, platforms, data spaces, society)
  • Customer relations, value propositions, and service exchange enabled by digital technologies
  • Role of digital technologies in real-world service scenarios

item.title: AI and the Future of Advertising Creativity
item.content:encoded:
Yung Kyun Choi, Dongguk University

Tae Hyun Baek, Sungkyunkwan University

This special issue examines how generative AI is transforming advertising creativity. Generative tools are shifting creative work from slow, expensive human-led processes to rapid, scalable production of copy, images, video, and message variants. This technological shift raises fundamental questions about how advertising creativity is imagined, produced, evaluated, and valued in an industry where creative advantage has long been central to competitive success.

The papers sought will investigate how AI affects each stage of creative work, from idea generation through asset production to personalization and variant creation. Beyond the mechanics of creative production, the issue addresses how agencies, brands, and platforms are reorganizing creative labor, which roles and skills remain valuable, and how business models built on production fees are being reshaped as marginal costs approach zero.

Appel publié par Journal of Advertising Research. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How does AI change the way creative ideas are generated, selected, and refined, and where in that process is human judgment most valuable?
  • When does AI assistance widen the range of creative directions a team explores, and when does it narrow it?
  • How should briefs, brainstorming, and creative workflows be redesigned around generative tools?
  • What is the most effective division of labor between human creatives and AI across ideation, drafting, and refinement?
  • How does near-zero marginal cost production change what advertising creative gets made, and how much of it?
  • What is gained and lost when finished assets are generated rather than crafted?
  • How does AI-produced creative compare with human-produced work on effectiveness, quality, and cost (for example, click-through, attention, and brand lift)?
  • How does production at scale change media planning, creative testing, and iteration?
  • How does generative AI change dynamic creative optimization and one-to-one message tailoring?
  • How can brands produce thousands of variants without eroding distinctiveness and brand consistency?
  • When does personalized AI creative outperform a single strong idea, and when does it not?
  • How do consumers respond to creative that is visibly machine-tailored to them?
  • How are agencies, in-house teams, and platforms reorganizing creative labor around AI?
  • Which creative roles and skills are being automated, augmented, or newly created?
  • How does AI reshape the agency and client relationship, the pitch process, and value capture?
  • What happens to agency business models when the cost of production approaches zero?
  • Does AI change how creativity is defined, judged, and rewarded in advertising?
  • How should originality, distinctiveness, and craft be valued when execution becomes commoditized?
  • Does widespread AI use homogenize advertising creative, and how can brands resist sameness?
  • How should creative awards, evaluation standards, and quality benchmarks adapt?
  • What methods (field experiments, computational and multimodal analysis, large-scale A/B testing) best capture the effect of AI on creative outcomes?
  • How can creativity itself be measured at scale across large volumes of AI-generated work?
  • How can researchers study homogenization, distinctiveness, and the diversity of creative output?
  • When does AI-generated creative help or hurt brand building and long-term equity, and what guardrails keep it on-brand and effective?

Timeline

  • January 15, 2027: GMC Tokyo 2027 submission deadline
  • September 1, 2027: Special issue submission window opens
  • October 15, 2027: Special issue manuscript deadline

item.title: Creativity and copyright in the shadow of GenAI: Managing and organizing creative content in the digitalization frenzy
item.content:encoded:
Konstantin Hondros, Helmut Schmidt University/University of the Armed Forces Hamburg

Leonhard Dobusch, University of Innsbruck

Astrid Mager, Austrian Academy of Sciences Vienna

Patricia Aufderheide, American University Washington

Patrick Cohendet, HEC Montréal

This special issue addresses the intersection of creativity, copyright, and generative AI within organizational and management contexts. As GenAI technology rapidly generates novel content across various forms, it raises critical questions about copyright management, ownership rights, and creative practices that have previously remained underexplored in management and organizational literature. The call seeks to examine how regulatory uncertainty and rapid technological development create both opportunities and challenges for creative work.

The editors invite empirical and conceptual research exploring how organizations navigate copyright and creativity amid GenAI adoption. Contributions are welcome from diverse disciplines including management, media studies, cultural studies, sociology, and science and technology studies, and from various fields potentially affected by GenAI such as creative industries, journalism, digital platforms, and scientific research. The special issue aims to make copyright a more accessible research topic and foster an interdisciplinary community examining creativity management in the context of emerging digitalization.

Appel publié par Innovation. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Creativity in the shadow of GenAI: How does GenAI affect the creation and management of creative content? How do creative and artistic practices change through GenAI use? What role does copyright play in creative transformations?
  • Doing copyright: How does GenAI foster copyright-related practices within and across organizations? Who are the actors and actants doing copyright in GenAI contexts? How are these practices shaping the organization of creativity? How is emerging GenAI regulation affecting organizations and creativity?
  • Conflicts over copyright: How do conflicts over copyright foster or impede creativity? What is the role of digitization in these conflicts and their evolution with GenAI? How do these conflicts affect organizational creativity and technological innovation management?
  • Inequality and copyright: How does GenAI affect access to knowledge within and across organizations? Who owns copyright and how does GenAI influence ownership structures? What are the consequences of copyright inequality for creativity?
  • Alternatives to copyright: What are alternatives to exclusive copyright regimes in GenAI contexts? How do commons-based and knowledge-sharing approaches challenge or facilitate the management and organization of creativity?
  • Researching copyright: What are methodologically promising ways to investigate the interrelation between copyright and creativity in organization and management? What are specific obstacles in the GenAI context?

item.content:encoded:

This special issue examines how Generative AI and Large Language Models are transforming financial modelling and applications. It welcomes research that explores AI's impact on traditional finance areas including asset pricing, financial intermediation, markets and investment, behavioral finance, banking, accounting, and insurance. The editors are particularly interested in work addressing ethical implications, financial inclusion benefits, and regulatory changes driven by these technologies.

The rapid adoption of tools like ChatGPT has sparked renewed interest in AI applications within finance. While Generative AI shows promise for enhancing data generation, analysis, decision-making, and risk management, research on its modelling and applications remains nascent. Simultaneously, significant challenges have emerged around data privacy, regulatory frameworks, innovation disruption, and the need to maintain human-centered approaches in financial systems.

item.title: Agentic and Generative AI in Healthcare Organizations: Governance, Clinical Workflow Integration and Responsible Value Creation
item.content:encoded:
This Journal of Enterprise Information Management Special Issue seeks to understand Agentic Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI (GenAI) in healthcare, and how these technologies impact the governance, strategy, and value creation of healthcare organizations. In technological innovation, digital technologies are reconfiguring value creation processes and prompting organizations to develop new adaptive strategies. In healthcare, this transformation is driving the adoption of innovative solutions to enhance value for stakeholders while supporting more personalised, predictive, and preventive models of care. AI and GenAI are emerging as strategic levers for optimising resource allocation, supporting new care delivery paradigms, and accelerating research and development. The rapid emergence of Agentic AI systems introduces a further step in this transformation, with AI technologies moving from reactive tools towards semi-autonomous systems able to plan, coordinate and monitor actions across complex organizations.

Appel publié par Journal of Enterprise Information Management. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How are GenAI and Agentic AI reshaping clinical, administrative, and managerial workflows in healthcare organizations?
  • How do healthcare organizations govern Agentic AI systems across care pathways?
  • What organizational capabilities are needed to move from experimental GenAI applications to integrated and scalable Agentic healthcare systems?
  • How can healthcare organizations ensure meaningful human oversight when AI systems become more autonomous, proactive, and embedded in clinical or administrative processes?
  • How do GenAI and agentic AI create, capture, or potentially destroy value for different healthcare stakeholders?
  • How do Agentic and GenAI systems transform healthcare knowledge management?

  • How do GenAI and Agentic AI affect decision-making processes within healthcare organizations?
  • How can healthcare organizations manage risks related to automation bias, inequitable outcomes and over-reliance on AI?
  • How do agentic AI and GenAI support healthcare system sustainability?

item.title: Beyond the Code: Understanding How, When and Why Humans Employ Generative AI in Innovation
item.content:encoded:
William Y. Degbey, University of Vaasa

Maria Pajuoja, University of Vaasa

Matti Pihlajamaa, VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland

Baniyelme D. Zoogah, McMaster University

Waymond Rodgers, University of Texas

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is defined as the frontier of computational advancements that references human intelligence in addressing ever more complex decision-making problems. A key development is Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, which can process and generate human-like language, extract insights, and produce creative outputs. Gen AI has enormous potential to significantly boost national economies. Its widespread adoption could increase GDP in the EU region by +8% (EUR 1.2–1.4 trillion) over the next ten years, provided innovators are equipped with the necessary skills and capabilities.

Yet, adoption remains uneven. For instance, European countries average a 54 percent adoption rate, below the global average of 61 percent. This uneven adoption is compounded by the global competition for skilled talent and persistent workforce shortages, particularly in digital and AI-related fields. McKinsey estimates that up to 12 million job transitions may be required due to AI, underscoring the urgent need for reskilling and entrepreneurial innovation.

Appel publié par Journal of Managerial Psychology. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How is Gen AI being used in innovation processes at different levels?
  • How do organizations apply Gen AI to replace, reinforce, or reveal innovation activities, and what are the resulting effects on, for example, process efficiency, novelty, and responsiveness to market needs?
  • How do varied patterns of Gen AI use across process phases and organizational levels influence the dynamics and management of innovation processes?
  • How do individual innovators use Gen AI in their work, what influences this usage, and what are the measurable outcomes of AI-augmented innovation efforts in terms of product, service, or process quality and speed?
  • In what ways does Gen AI influence innovation team dynamics, including collaboration, resilience, and decision-making, particularly in virtual or hybrid team environments?
  • What psychological and behavioral effects emerge from using Gen AI in innovation settings, such as changes in employee engagement, collaboration dynamics, or perceptions of autonomy?
  • How do managerial competencies influence the successful implementation of Gen AI in organizational innovation efforts?
  • What organizational capabilities need to be developed to successfully implement, integrate, and support the use of Gen AI in innovation efforts?
  • How are organizations supporting continuous learning and skill development for employees working with Gen AI, and what mechanisms are most effective in enabling the strategic use of Gen AI?
  • What ethical challenges do organizations face when deploying Gen AI in innovation activities, and how are they addressing issues such as intellectual property, transparency, and sociocultural responsibility?

item.title: Theoretical perspectives on Generative and Agentic AI adoption in service environments
item.content:encoded:
Mark Camilleri, University of Malta

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) are transforming how services are designed, delivered, experienced and led. While GenAI refers to systems, such as large language models (LLMs), that produce content in response to human prompts; Agentic AI technologies may be considered as active agents that can implement tasks (rather than merely functioning as passive generators). The latter can monitor situations, allocate resources, initiate and manage processes as well as co-ordinate multiple activities. Hence, Agentic AI algorithms and their governance affect service outcomes.
